section.p: NGINX is deliberately static: its configuration is read once at startup (or reload) and compiled into kernel-level data structures. This rigidity is a feature — it makes nginx predictable, fast, and easy to reason about — but it creates friction whenever runtime adaptability is required: upstream weights that need to track backend health scores, virtual hosts generated from a tenant database, SSL certificates that rotate on a schedule, or request routing rules that depend on live feature-flag state.

NGINX JS DOM embeds QuickJS [https://bellard.org/quickjs/] (a lightweight ES2020+ [https://tc39.es/ecma262/2020/] JavaScript engine) directly into nginx and exposes the entire nginx configuration as a structured JavaScript object tree called the Configuration Object Model (COM). Through the COM, JavaScript can:
Read the full live configuration of every module in every server and location.

Write configuration properties — upstream peer weights, SSL certificates, location directives, gzip settings, and much more — with immediate effect, either for the current worker or atomically for all workers at once.

Generate server and location blocks at parse time, before nginx has even finished reading its configuration file, and at run-time, when traffic events are processed by nginx workers in their nginx event loops.
Handle requests in JavaScript, using the same event-driven async model as nginx itself.
Offload CPU-intensive work to background threads (Workers) without blocking the nginx event loop.
Maintain shared mutable state across all nginx worker processes using SharedWorkers and SharedArrayBuffers.
The result is an nginx that can be programmed rather than merely configured — without restarting, without patching C code, and without sacrificing the performance or stability of the core server.
This manual assumes:

Familiarity with nginx configuration syntax and core concepts (workers, upstreams, locations, modules). See the NGINX Beginner’s Guide [https://nginx.org/en/docs/beginners_guide.html] and the full module reference [https://nginx.org/en/docs] if you need a refresher.

Working knowledge of modern JavaScript (ES2020): async/await, Promises, import/export, SharedArrayBuffer, Atomics. See the ECMAScript 2020 specification [https://tc39.es/ecma262/2020/] or any ES2020 reference.
You do not need to know C or QuickJS internals to use the JS DOM API.

title.p: A Map of the Moving Parts

section.p: The sections that follow cover these components:
Component │ What it gives you

js_preprocess │ Runs JavaScript during config parsing; the script writes config text back into the parser. Use it to generate server/location blocks from files, environment variables, or external sources.
js_init_http │ Runs JavaScript after the http {} block is parsed but before directives are merged. Can read already-parsed servers and inject new ones.

js_source │ Evaluates JavaScript in the master process after all config has been parsed. This is where you install request handlers, set up Workers and SharedWorkers, and perform any pre-fork initialisation.
Request handlers │ JavaScript async functions assigned to location.handler. Each request runs through the nginx event loop; await suspends the handler without blocking any other request.
COM │ The nginx global object tree. Read live config values; write mutations that take effect immediately.
Workers │ Standard Web Worker API. A per-nginx-worker background thread for CPU-bound work. Does not block the event loop.
SharedWorkers │ A single long-lived thread in the master process, connected to every nginx worker via UNIX sockets. The canonical place for mutable state that must be consistent across all workers.

SharedArrayBuffers + Atomics │ Binary shared-memory regions (MDN reference) accessible from any thread with zero copy. Combined with Atomics, they enable lock-free counters, mutexes, and condition variables.
Accept control │ nginx.suspendAcceptance() / nginx.suspendAllWorkers() — pause connection acceptance during a mutation window, then resume.
Resource limits │ nginx.workerMemoryLimit and nginx.workerRequestTimeout cap heap usage and CPU time per request; JS exceptions are caught; the worker survives.

section.p: Key properties of this topology:
Each nginx worker process has its own independent JS runtime. QuickJS is not thread-safe; no runtime is ever shared between processes.

Workers inherit the master’s runtime via copy-on-write after fork(). Scripts do not need to be re-evaluated; all handler functions, SharedWorker references, and global variables are ready immediately.

SharedWorkers run in the master process as pthreads, outside any worker. Each worker communicates with a SharedWorker over a dedicated UNIX socket channel. This is the only channel through which workers can share mutable JS state.
JS Workers (lowercase) are pthreads spawned inside a worker process. They exist to offload work from the event loop and are private to their nginx worker.
All COM mutations go through one of three scopes:
Scope │ Mechanism │ Visible to
Per-request snapshot │ r.location.setWriteMode("local") — writes a per-request copy of the location config │ This request only; reversed when the request pool is freed
This worker only │ Direct COM write (default) │ All subsequent requests on this worker process
All workers atomically │ await nginx.suspendAllWorkers() → mutate → await nginx.resumeAllWorkers() │ All workers, once they resume
This section goes from "hello world" to "live upstream rebalancing" in four steps, each building on the previous one.

section.p: : Multiple async handlers can be suspended concurrently on the same worker. Each nginx worker runs a single-threaded event loop; async handlers cooperate by yielding at every await point, allowing other requests to be accepted and served in between. Use Workers or SharedWorkers when you need true CPU parallelism or need to share mutable state across workers.

section.p: js_preprocess runs synchronously inside the C parse loop. There is no event loop at this stage, so the standard req.fetch() API is unavailable. The std.urlGet() function (QuickJS std library [https://bellard.org/quickjs/quickjs.html#Standard-library]) works around this by spawning curl as a child process and blocking until the response arrives.
curl must be installed on the system.

// Uses std.urlGet() which shells out to curl — blocking and synchronous.
// Fail loudly — a bad config is worse than a failed start.

section.p: : std.urlGet always spawns a curl subprocess. For reliability in production, prefer writing config data to a file during a pre-start hook and reading it with std.loadFile(), keeping js_preprocess independent of network availability at start time. The network fetch pattern is useful for short-lived tooling or environments where the config service is guaranteed to be reachable.

JS Workers are background pthreads spawned inside an nginx worker process. They implement the standard Web Worker API [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Worker] and are the correct tool when a request needs to perform CPU-intensive computation without blocking the event loop.
Each nginx worker process has its own set of Workers; they are not shared between nginx workers.

A SharedWorker [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SharedWorker] is a single long-lived pthread running in the nginx master process, connected to every nginx worker via dedicated UNIX socket channels. Unlike JS Workers (one per nginx worker), there is exactly one SharedWorker instance regardless of the worker_processes count.
This makes SharedWorkers the canonical location for:
Session stores — a token → user mapping visible to every worker.
Distributed rate limiters — accurate global request-per-second counting.
Feature flags — a single flag store; updates propagate to all workers on the next message.
Distributed locks — a central lock arbiter that any worker can acquire.
Config broadcast — push a config change to all workers simultaneously (see [scope-2-all-workers-atomically]).
Use this pattern when a worker needs a dedicated two-way channel with the SharedWorker (i.e. replies must go back to the same worker that sent the request):

section.p: A SharedArrayBuffer [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/SharedArrayBuffer] is a region of memory accessible — with zero copying — from any thread: nginx workers, JS Workers, and the SharedWorker thread.

Typed array views (Int32Array, Float64Array, BigInt64Array, etc.) over a SAB provide direct read/write access. Atomics [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Atomics] operations (add, compareExchange, wait, notify) provide the synchronisation primitives needed for safe concurrent access.
A SAB created in js_source is backed by the CoW page mapping inherited by every worker after fork(). All workers share the same physical pages.

section.p: A SAB created inside a request handler (post-fork) is backed by a Linux memfd and can be transferred to a JS Worker or SharedWorker via postMessage. The receiving thread `mmap`s the same file descriptor, establishing a shared mapping without copying data.

section.p: : Atomics.waitAsync (non-blocking, returns a Promise) is available in the nginx event loop context and is the correct way to wait for a SAB value to change from the main thread.

COM mutations applied directly from a handler affect only the worker that executed the handler. Other workers have independent CoW copies and will not see the change. Furthermore, if a mutation is applied while another request on the same worker is halfway through using the old value, the result can be inconsistent.
Accept control solves both problems by temporarily pausing connection acceptance, creating a window during which no new requests can start and the worker is in a known-clean state.
These are synchronous, instant, and affect only the calling worker.

stanza.v: // Stop accepting new connections on THIS worker.
// OS backlog holds new connections; other workers keep accepting normally.
// Apply a batch of mutations atomically from this worker's perspective.

section.p: While any or all workers have acceptance suspended, incoming TCP connections queue in the OS SYN/accept backlog:
Backlog size is controlled by net.core.somaxconn (typically 128–4096) and the listen directive’s backlog=N parameter.
If the backlog fills before resumeAcceptance() is called, the kernel drops new SYN packets. From the client’s perspective this looks like the server is temporarily unavailable.
For short mutation windows (sub-millisecond), the probability of backlog overflow is negligible even under high load.

: Do not hold all workers suspended for long operations (database queries, external HTTP calls). Complete all blocking work before calling suspendAllWorkers(), then apply changes synchronously in the mutation window.

section.p: Config data is written to a file by an external process (deploy script, Kubernetes operator, config management tool) and read synchronously during nginx startup:
This runs on every nginx -s reload, so the file is the single source of truth.

See the example in [example-fetching-config-from-a-network-service]. Use this pattern for tooling environments where network availability is guaranteed. In production, pre-download to a file during a health-check or init-container step to avoid coupling nginx startup to network availability.

section.p: When a JS allocation exceeds the limit, QuickJS throws RangeError: out of memory. The worker process remains healthy; the individual request receives a 500 error.

stanza.v: const huge = new ArrayBuffer(512 * 1024 * 1024); // exceeds limit
// e is RangeError: out of memory

section.p: nginx.workerRequestTimeout sets the maximum wall-clock time (in milliseconds) a single JS handler invocation may consume. If the handler runs longer than this (including time spent in a tight synchronous loop), QuickJS fires an interrupt that aborts the handler. The worker survives and the request receives HTTP 500.

stanza.v: // Allow each handler at most 5 seconds of wall time.
// Re-configure at runtime from a handler.

section.p: JavaScript exceptions in a handler are caught by the module framework and converted to HTTP 500 responses. The worker process never crashes due to an unhandled JS exception.

stanza.v: // This exception is caught by the framework — worker stays up.
// Client receives: HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error

section.p: The JS runtime runs inside an nginx worker process (or master, for SharedWorkers) with the same OS privileges. The following restrictions apply:
No access to nginx’s internal C memory outside the COM API. There is no ctypes, ffi, or equivalent.
No subprocess spawning from handlers or SharedWorkers. The os.exec() function from QuickJS os is available only in Workers and js_preprocess scripts, not in nginx event-loop handlers.
Blocking the event loop with a synchronous tight loop is interrupted by the request timeout if nginx.workerRequestTimeout is set.
Atomics.wait (blocking) must not be called from the event loop; use Atomics.waitAsync (non-blocking, returns a Promise) instead.
Directive │ Context │ Arguments │ Description

js_source path │ main │ 1 (path) │ Evaluate path in the master process after config parsing (init_conf). Multiple allowed; evaluated in declaration order. The JS runtime created here is inherited by all workers after fork.

js_preprocess path │ main │ 1 (path) │ Evaluate path immediately when encountered during ngx_conf_parse. Receives global config.write(text). Multiple allowed; each runs in an isolated ephemeral runtime.
js_init_http path │ http │ 1 (path) │ Evaluate path after the http {} block finishes parsing, before merge. Receives config.write(text) and read-only nginx.http.servers[].

JS DOM implements a subset of the standard Web Worker and SharedWorker APIs.
API │ Notes
new Worker(url) │ Spawn a JS Worker thread. url is a path to a JS file.
worker.postMessage(data [, transferList]) │ Send a value to the Worker. Transferable: ArrayBuffer. Shareable: SharedArrayBuffer.
worker.onmessage = fn │ Receive a value from the Worker.
worker.terminate() │ Stop the Worker thread.
new SharedWorker(url) │ Connect to (or create) a SharedWorker. Returns an object with a port property.
sw.port.postMessage(data) │ Send to the SharedWorker.
sw.port.onmessage = fn │ Receive from the SharedWorker.
onconnect = fn (in SW script) │ Fires when a new worker process connects. e.ports[0] is the port.
onmessage = fn (in SW script) │ Global handler; fires for any message from any worker. clients array is available.
clients (in SW script) │ Array of all connected port objects; use for broadcast.
Operation │ Event loop │ JS Worker │ SharedWorker │ js_preprocess
new SharedArrayBuffer(n) │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Typed array read/write │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Atomics.load/store/add/… │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Atomics.compareExchange │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Atomics.wait (blocking) │ ✗ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Atomics.waitAsync │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✗
Atomics.notify │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓
Transfer via postMessage │ ✓ │ ✓ │ ✓ │ —

: Never call Atomics.wait from the nginx event loop — it blocks the thread, preventing all request processing. Use Atomics.waitAsync in the event loop and Atomics.wait in Workers / SharedWorker threads.
